sections.h2: What is property tax like in Bath County, Kentucky?
sections.html:
Bath County is a rural county of about 279 square miles on the eastern edge of the Bluegrass, and its property tax is run from a few courthouse offices in Owingsville. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) values land and houses, the sheriff collects the bill, and the county clerk records deeds and receives unpaid bills.

The county was cut from Montgomery County in 1811 and is named for mineral springs once credited with healing powers. Owingsville is the seat and the largest city, with Salt Lick and Sharpsburg the other two cities. A fire set by Union troops destroyed the Owingsville courthouse in 1864, and the county is known for the Kentucky Meat Shower of March 3, 1876, when an unidentified substance fell from the sky. Neighbors are Fleming, Rowan, Menifee, Montgomery, Bourbon and Nicholas counties.

Interstate 64 crosses the county, and Cave Run Lake and the Daniel Boone National Forest take up a large share of its land, which limits where homes can be built.

sections.h2: How many people and homes does Bath County have?
sections.html:
Bath grew from 11,591 people in 2010 to 12,750 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate of 13,176 adds another 3.4 percent. The 2020 count found 5,445 housing units with 10.4 percent of them vacant, and every resident lived in a rural area.

The Bureau's five year figures, covering 2020 through 2024, fill in the market:

  • The typical owned home is valued at $129,800, and three in four homes (74.7 percent) have an owner living in them.
  • Median gross rent is $659 a month.
  • Median household income is $56,541, while 22.6 percent of residents fall below the poverty line.
  • A worker's mean trip to a job takes 30.0 minutes, the longest of the four Kentucky counties in these Census tables.
  • Zero building permits were logged for 2025.

With almost no new construction, the houses that change hands here are mostly old ones. Age brings deferred repairs, and a PVA record that was never updated can overstate or understate a house.

sections.h2: Which Bath County office does what?
sections.html:
The county site lists elected offices with courthouse contacts. Every one sits in Owingsville, and mail goes to separate post office boxes, so address a payment or an appeal to the right office.

  • PVA at (606) 674-6382: assessments, exemption forms and appeal conferences.
  • Sheriff at (606) 674-2931: tax bills and collection.
  • County Clerk at (606) 674-2613: deeds, mortgages, liens and bills that turn delinquent after April 15.
  • County Attorney: notices and payment plans on delinquent bills.

The clerk's site also carries a page of delinquent taxes, handy for checking whether a parcel is listed.

sections.h2: How many people and homes does Bath County have?
sections.html:
The 2020 Census counted 12,750 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is 13,176, a gain of 3.4 percent. All of the population lives in rural areas, according to the Census count summarized by Wikipedia.

Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 give a picture of the market a seller faces:

  • Owner occupied homes are valued at a median of $129,800, and 74.7 percent of homes are owner occupied.
  • Median gross rent is $659 a month.
  • Median household income is $56,541, and 22.6 percent of residents are in poverty.
  • The mean travel time to work is 30.0 minutes, the longest among the four Kentucky counties in these Census tables, so a longer drive to work is part of daily life here.
  • No building permits were recorded in 2025.

With few new homes being built, older houses make up almost all of what sells in Bath County. Age brings deferred repairs, and a PVA record that has not been updated can overstate or understate what a house is worth.

sections.h2: How is a Bath County assessment appealed?
sections.html:
Ask the Bath County PVA for a conference while the roll is open in May. If you agree on a number, you are done. If not, you file at the clerk's office and state the value you claim.

The local board has three members and meets at the county seat under KRS 133.030. On day one it reviews recent sales of comparable homes and may visit disputed properties. It sits no more than five days without the Department of Revenue's approval, and its decision comes by certified mail.

  • Gather sales of similar homes from the past year, photos of defects, and any appraisal.
  • Ask the PVA to walk you through how recorded sales produced your value.
  • Bring a repair estimate if a roof, well or septic problem is missing from the record.

A tax bill cannot be contested, because the filing window closes months earlier.

sections.h2: Who can claim the homestead exemption in Bath County?
sections.html:
A Bath County owner who reaches 65, or who is totally disabled, can claim it for the home where they live. Apply at the PVA in the year you want it, with proof of age or disability.

KRS 132.810 allows one exemption per residential unit and counts a mobile home or manufactured house as a unit, which suits a county where many owners live in one. The amount follows the cost of living and is revisited every two years, so ask the PVA for the current figure. If you qualify after paying, the statute entitles you to a refund of the tax on the exempt amount. Report a sale or a death to the PVA, and the buyer or heir applies on their own.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Bath County taxes?
sections.html:
Once April 15 passes, the sheriff hands any unpaid bill to the clerk, who files it as a certificate of delinquency and a lien. Monthly interest of 1 percent starts, and the Department of Revenue's worked examples add commissions of 10 percent for the clerk and 20 percent for the county attorney.

Notices go out, the parcels are advertised, and a private buyer can purchase the certificate at a summer sale and tack on its own charges. KRS 134.015 makes the tax a personal debt of the person who owned on January 1 and lets the lien trail the property for 11 years.

sections.h2: What should a rural Bath County seller know about land and forest?
sections.html:
Many parcels here include acreage. Kentucky assesses working farmland at agricultural value, not market value, under Section 172A of the state constitution, and a buyer or lender will ask whether your land keeps that classification. Confirm it with the PVA before you list.

Federal land is exempt from property tax, and a good part of the county lies inside the Daniel Boone National Forest, so check that a boundary on a rural tract matches both the recorded deed and the PVA map.

An older house with repairs pending and a bill sitting at the clerk's office can still sell. The payoff comes from the proceeds at closing, and the clerk quotes it for the month. To weigh a cash offer against a listing, compare the net after repairs, back taxes and carrying costs.

faqs.q: Whom do I pay for Bath County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay the Bath County Sheriff in Owingsville, whose office the county site lists at (606) 674-2931. Bills are mailed in the fall.

faqs.q: When can a Bath County assessment be appealed?
faqs.a: Only while the tax roll is open for inspection in May. Meet the PVA first, then file with the clerk on the next business day after the period closes.

faqs.q: What is the typical home value in Bath County?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures give $129,800 for owned homes, with owners living in 74.7 percent of homes.

faqs.q: Is there a homestead exemption in Bath County?
faqs.a: Yes. An owner who is 65 or totally disabled can apply to the PVA under KRS 132.810 for the home they live in.

faqs.q: What happens when a Bath County bill reaches the clerk?
faqs.a: Interest and fees are added, and the bill can be sold to a private buyer at a summer sale. Ask the clerk for a payoff and the county attorney about a payment plan.
